author: @FrankCurzio
text: Love hearing this from someone actually doing the work. AI cuts both ways, to be seen how this places out long term...

author: @FrankCurzio
text:
I've been on Wall Street for 30+ years, and I'm not a cyber expert.

But I HAVE watched tech trends and big events my entire career, and I know what's serious and what's not.

This looks unprecedented, and the scale is what tells you that.

In just 48 hours, one tally counted 27 major hacks and security holes coming to light.

In a normal year, any ONE of them would be among the biggest cyber stories of the year. We got all of them in two days, hitting governments, banks, hospitals and grocery chains.

In June, the US and its closest allies warned about AI-powered hacking: "The timeline is not years, it is months."

In August, the NSA, FBI and three other agencies warned that hackers were using AI to break into the machines that run US factories, water and energy plants. Their words: "This is not a theoretical risk - it is an active threat."

Then came this week.

The biggest one is a hole in PHP, a programming language that runs about 70% of the websites on the internet.

Researchers found it using OpenAI's AI and quietly told the US government on Oct 16. The plan was to keep it secret until a fix was ready.

It didn't work.

Amazon says attackers were already using it the very next day, and nobody knows how they got it. The fix went public on Oct 21, but it showed everyone exactly where the hole was, so attacks exploded within hours. Germany, France, Finland and the Netherlands pulled government sites offline while they patched.

And Cisco estimates about half the public servers running PHP are too old to get the fix at all.

Then the keys started leaking.

Railway, a cloud platform used by about 2M developers, says hackers may have accessed its customers' secret keys. A smaller rival, Zeabur, lost data on 321,810 accounts and is shutting down for good.

And more and more, the hacking is being done by AI.

Microsoft says a China-aligned group used an AI tool to try to break into 2,000+ organizations at once. Reuters reported one hacker used AI agents to break into 100+ companies, for about $50 a break-in.

Now it's reaching the banks. JPMorgan, Bank of America and Wells Fargo are finding AI agents inside customer accounts that they can't account for, Axios reported.

But here's why the events of the last 48 hours are so critical:

For 30 years, what kept most of us safe was simple. Breaking in took rare, skilled people, and there weren't many of them.

AI just ended that shortage.

It finds the weak spots and breaks in on its own, around the clock. And Wall Street caught on fast.

On Oct 21, while everyone scrambled to patch, cyber stocks ripped. Cloudflare and Zscaler jumped about 7%, CrowdStrike 6%, Palo Alto 4%. The next day the Nasdaq fell over 2% on AI spending fears, and Palo Alto rose another 3%.

That move makes total sense to me. Companies can slow down their AI spending, and the market's scared they will. But after a week like this, no board in America is cutting its security budget. Morgan Stanley says those budgets were already growing.

And this isn't over. New attacks are coming to light every day.

I'll be tracking this every week and what it means for markets. Follow me @FrankCurzio so you don't miss it.
